title: What Do You Want Me to Do for You?
paragraphs:
What Do You Want Me to Do for You?
The Question That Exposes Every Heart, Reveals Every Wound, and Changes Every Life
There are moments in Scripture that seem so simple we almost miss their terrifying depth.
Then comes a question that feels almost unnecessary.
A question so obvious it almost sounds absurd.
Yet hidden inside it is one of the most life-changing conversations ever recorded.
A blind beggar named Bartimaeus sits beside the road outside Jericho. Dust fills the air. Crowds move around him. Voices rise and fall like waves. He cannot see faces, but he hears rumors.
Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.
For years Bartimaeus had likely heard stories.
And now Hope was walking past him.
"Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!"
The crowd immediately does what crowds often do.
They tell him to be quiet.
But pain that has met possibility cannot stay silent.
So he cries out even louder.
"Son of David, have mercy on me!"
The Creator of the universe halts His journey because one desperate voice refuses to stop calling His name.
The One holding galaxies together pauses for a blind beggar.
The One who sustains creation listens to a forgotten man sitting in the dirt.
The crowd may have ignored him.
The same people who were rebuking Bartimaeus moments earlier suddenly become messengers.
"Take heart. Get up. He is calling you."
Bartimaeus throws aside his cloak and runs toward Jesus.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
In Greek, the phrase appears as:

Τί σοι θέλεις ποιήσω;
(Ti soi theleis poiēsō?)
"What do you desire that I should do for you?"
At first glance the question seems unnecessary.
Because Jesus was never merely interested in fixing symptoms.
Jesus already knew what Bartimaeus needed.
The question was not for Jesus.
God often asks questions not because He lacks information but because we lack revelation.
Not because God could not find Adam.
Jesus asks questions that uncover the soul.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
For perhaps the first time in years, Bartimaeus is invited to speak his deepest desire aloud.
Not what others think he should want.
"Rabboni, that I may regain my sight."
Bartimaeus is not approaching Jesus as a magician.
Faith is not merely believing Jesus can do something.
Faith is trusting who He is.
"Go your way; your faith has made you well."
And he follows Jesus on the road.
But the deeper miracle is often overlooked.
The healing happened after the confession.
This is where the story collides with us.
Because Jesus still asks the same question today.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
Many of us would rather answer with religious clichés.
And while surrender is biblical, Jesus often presses deeper.
Because beneath our church language are hidden realities.
Many believers have become experts at pretending.
We know how to look strong.
We know how to sound spiritual.
We know how to smile while bleeding internally.
But Jesus does not heal the version of us we perform.
He heals the version of us we surrender.
That is why this question can feel uncomfortable.
If Jesus stood before you right now and asked:
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
Would you ask Him to heal your marriage?
Restore your relationship with your children?
Or would you stand silent because you have lived with your pain so long that you no longer believe healing is possible?
Many people stop asking because disappointment taught them to stop expecting.
Yet Bartimaeus teaches us something profound.
Faith keeps calling even when crowds keep criticizing.
Faith keeps believing when circumstances remain unchanged.
Faith keeps crying out when silence seems louder than answers.
The story becomes even more powerful when we notice something remarkable.
Just a few verses earlier, Jesus asked the exact same question to James and John.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
The identical question exposed radically different priorities.
When Jesus asks us what we want, our answer often reveals what truly rules our hearts.
The question is not merely about receiving blessings.
Because the greatest miracle in the story was not eyesight.
Many people can see physically and remain spiritually blind.
The greatest miracle was that Bartimaeus recognized who Jesus truly was.
Bartimaeus saw the Son of David.
The blind man saw more than the sighted crowd.
And perhaps that is the scandalous beauty of grace.
The people society overlooks often recognize Jesus more clearly than those who think they have everything together.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Every one of us is Bartimaeus.
But because mercy heard our cry.
This is why the cross changes everything.
At Calvary, Jesus took the blindness of humanity upon Himself.
The judgment we deserved fell on Him.
The grace we did not deserve flowed to us.
The Gospel is not a story about good people finding God.
It is a story about a holy God stopping for broken people.
This is why no scandal is too great.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The woman at the well carried a broken history.
And perhaps today Jesus is stopping for you.
As you read these words, He asks the same question He asked Bartimaeus.
"What do you want Me to do for you?"
The miracle often begins when the mask finally comes off.
And if this message exposed something hidden inside you, be honest.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Through your support, more souls hear about Jesus, more believers are strengthened, and more lives are impacted by biblical truth.
One desperate cry stopped the Savior on the road to Jerusalem—and your cry is not too small for Him to hear today.
